analysis.one_liner: Cuts taxes for families, seniors, and investors while freezing Medicare provider payments and capping federal spending.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 246-188 on April 5, 1995, but the Senate Finance Committee, which held hearings in June, never brought it to a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This was the tax bill from the House Republican 'Contract with America.' It would have created a $500 credit for each child under 18, a small credit for married couples, tax-free savings accounts for buying a first home or paying for college, repeal of the 1993 tax increase on Social Security benefits, and a 50% deduction on capital gains, plus relief from the corporate minimum tax and higher estate tax exemptions. To help pay for it, the bill froze Medicare payment updates to nursing homes and home health agencies, raised retirement contributions for federal workers and Members of Congress, capped annual federal spending through 2000, and made its own tax cuts take effect only if a companion budget actually balanced by 2002. The House passed it, but the Senate never voted.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with children under 18 would get a $500-per-child credit, phasing out only above $200,000 of income. Married couples would get a credit of up to $145 to offset the marriage penalty. Higher-income retirees would keep more of their Social Security once the tax on benefits was repealed after 1999. Investors would deduct half their capital gains, with inflation indexing on assets held over three years, and corporations would see the alternative minimum tax phased out to zero and an alternative capital gains rate cut from 35% to 25%. Adoptive parents would get a credit up to $5,000, caregivers a $500 credit, and savers could use new 'American Dream Savings Accounts' tax-free for first homes, college, or medical costs. Small businesses would get larger expensing limits and clearer home-office deductions.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a $500 tax credit per child under 18, phasing out above $200,000 of income, effective for tax years after 1995.
Allows a credit of up to $145 to reduce the marriage penalty for joint filers.
Repeals the 1993 increase in the tax on Social Security benefits, phasing it down from 1996 and terminating the tax entirely after December 31, 1999.
Allows non-corporate taxpayers to deduct 50% of net capital gains and indexes the basis of assets held more than three years to inflation.
Phases out the corporate alternative minimum tax to zero after 2000 and cuts the alternative capital gains tax on corporations from 35% to 25%.
Provides a tax credit of up to $5,000 for qualified adoption expenses (phased down above $60,000 of income) and a $500 credit for taxpayers keeping a person requiring custodial care in the household.
Establishes 'American Dream Savings Accounts' whose qualified withdrawals are tax-free when used for a first home, higher education, or medical expenses.
Raises the monthly exempt amount in the Social Security earnings test so retirees at or above retirement age can earn more without losing benefits.

analysis.who_pays: The Treasury would lose revenue from the tax cuts, with the deficit risk falling on future taxpayers. The bill's offsets come from freezing Medicare payment updates to skilled nursing facilities and home health agencies, permanently setting the Medicare Part B premium at 50% of the monthly actuarial rate for enrollees 65 and over, and raising retirement contribution rates for federal employees and Members of Congress to as much as 9.5% of pay. The spending limits in Title I would force across-the-board cuts if discretionary spending exceeded the caps.

drawbacks.text: None of the family tax cuts would take effect unless the FY1996 budget resolution called for a balanced budget by FY2002 and the reconciliation bill actually achieved the needed deficit reduction, so the help for ordinary families was conditional on a separate process.

The capital gains deduction, inflation indexing, corporate AMT phaseout, and higher estate and gift tax credits concentrate their value on high-income households and corporations, and the revenue loss adds to the deficit.
The repeal of the tax on Social Security benefits mainly benefits higher-income retirees, since lower-income beneficiaries already owe little or no tax on their benefits.

Freezing updates to Medicare payment limits for skilled nursing facilities and home health agencies (for cost periods beginning in FY1994-1995 and mid-1994 to mid-1996) holds down what those providers are paid, which providers warned could squeeze care capacity.

Federal employees and Members of Congress would see their retirement contributions rise incrementally to 9.5% of pay (10% for law enforcement, firefighters, and air traffic controllers), a direct pay cut, and Members would lose the option to opt out of the newer retirement system.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The broad middle-class pieces — the child credit, marriage-penalty credit, adoption credit, and savings accounts — would deliver real, immediate help to ordinary families, and the bill notably raises its own sponsors' retirement contributions rather than shielding them. But the largest dollar items (the capital gains deduction, indexing, estate tax credit increases, and corporate AMT repeal) flow mostly to wealthy households and corporations, and the bill never fully pays for them: the family credits are contingent on a separate balanced-budget process, the offsets lean heavily on freezing Medicare provider payments, and the discretionary caps would force automatic spending cuts if exceeded. The 'deficit reduction' half of the title rests partly on projections and enforcement rules rather than guaranteed offsets.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 246-188, but the Senate Finance Committee — which held hearings in June 1995 — never reported it, and the House's last action pointed further work to a separate budget bill, H.R. 2491.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Archer, chairman of the Ways and Means Committee, introduced the bill on March 13, 1995; the committee ordered it reported the next day by a 21-14 vote and reported it on March 21.

The Rules Committee structured debate so the bill was amended into a substitute combining the tax cuts with spending caps, FCC auction authority, privatization of the U.S. Enrichment Corporation, federal retirement changes, and Medicare savings.
Minority Leader Richard Gephardt moved to recommit the bill with instructions; the motion failed 168-265, with 166 of 204 Democrats in favor and 228 of 229 Republicans opposed.

Rep. James Moran raised a point of order that parts of the bill raised taxes and so needed a three-fifths majority; the chair overruled him, and the House tabled his appeal 228-204 on a nearly perfect party-line vote.
Final passage passed 246-188: Republicans voted 219-11 in favor, Democrats 27-176 against.

The Senate received the bill on April 6, 1995, and referred it to the Finance Committee, which held hearings on June 7 and June 19 but never reported it; on October 26, 1995, the House recorded that further action was on H.R. 2491, a separate reconciliation bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the Senate never voted and no provision became law, families never received the child or marriage credits and investors never got the capital gains cut — but the Treasury also avoided the revenue loss, and Medicare nursing homes and home health agencies avoided the payment freezes. The 1995 tax fight moved instead into H.R. 2491, where it was resolved separately.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury and Medicare providers; families got nothing

sides.party_line_note: Final passage split sharply by party — Republicans 219-11 for, Democrats 27-176 against — and the vote to table the tax-increase point of order was 228-0 Republicans to 0-203 Democrats.

industries.note: The bill would let individuals deduct half their capital gains, index asset bases to inflation, cut the corporate alternative capital gains rate, phase out the corporate AMT, and raise estate and gift tax credits. These benefits concentrate at the top of the income scale, and the revenue loss adds to deficits future taxpayers must cover.

The bill freezes Medicare per-diem limits and prospective payments by barring consideration of cost changes from FY1994-1995 cost periods. Facilities would receive smaller payment increases, which helps the Treasury but pressures the facilities' finances.
The bill freezes Medicare cost limits for home health services for cost periods beginning July 1994 through July 1996. Agencies' Medicare revenue growth would be held down.

The bill gives qualified long-term care insurance favorable tax treatment as health insurance, lets IRA and employer plan withdrawals pay premiums tax-free, and treats payments to unlicensed relatives as non-medical. That builds a tax-preferred market for private long-term care policies while making family caregivers outside the licensed system less favored.

The bill allows accelerated death benefit riders and excludes from income amounts paid to terminally or chronically ill policyholders, making life insurance products more useful to sick policyholders.

industries.industry: Federal employees and Members of Congress
industries.note: Retirement contribution rates rise incrementally to 9.5% of pay (10% for law enforcement, firefighters, and air traffic controllers), annuities are computed over more years, and Members lose the option to opt out of the newer retirement system. Notably, the bill raises officeholders' own contributions rather than shielding them.

The bill provides for privatizing the federally owned U.S. Enrichment Corporation, transferring its assets to private investors while the U.S. remains liable for pre-privatization operations and accepts the corporation's radioactive waste. The government operation becomes a private business, with taxpayers retaining legacy liabilities.
